reason: The run is consistent: all three occurrences read "down payment". That is a departure from the traditional "earnest", though, and from the "guarantee", "pledge" and "deposit" of most modern versions. Because competent translators split several ways on this word and each chapter is translated blind, an entry is warranted to fix the departure and prevent drift in later runs, not to repair an inconsistency in this one.
sense: a first payment that secures a transaction and commits the payer to the rest; used figuratively of the Spirit given to believers
rationale: In the commercial Greek of the period the word meant money paid in advance that both forms part of the full payment and binds the payer to complete it. "Earnest" in this sense is no longer understood by modern readers, and "guarantee" or "pledge" conveys the assurance but loses the idea that part of the thing itself has already been handed over. "Down payment" is ordinary modern English that keeps both ideas, and standard lexicons list it among the glosses.
standard_view: The KJV has "earnest". Modern versions divide: ESV and NKJV use "guarantee", NASB "pledge", NIV "deposit" with "guaranteeing" added, NRSV "first installment" in 2 Corinthians and "pledge" in Ephesians, and CSB and NET "down payment". Scholars agree it is a commercial loanword from Semitic for earnest money or a deposit; in the Septuagint of Genesis 38 it is a pledge that is later returned, so some prefer "pledge", but the part-payment sense is the common commercial one and fits Paul's use of the Spirit as a first share of what is to come.
